summary:
MarqLens is a Streamlit data explorer built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective". It shows how annual rainfall in the Amazon River basin changed from 2001 to 2024, using NASA GPM IMERG Final V07 data retrieved through Giovanni.
For every grid cell, MarqLens answers the challenge's four questions. It shows what is changing (rainfall) and where (on an interactive map). It shows how much (Sen's slope in mm per year) and whether the change is significant (Mann-Kendall with Hamed-Rao correction, plus Benjamini-Yekutieli control). Results are worded in three plain-language tiers, and grey areas mark places where the evidence is too weak.
The south-central basin and the Andean strip show signs of drying. However, 24 years of data cannot separate the extreme dry years of 2022–2024 from a lasting shift, and MarqLens shows this uncertainty openly. Links to El Niño and Atlantic sea temperatures are presented as associations, not causes.
The analysis runs on trendlab, an open, tested Python package that can be reused for other variables and regions.
details:
What it does and how it works
MarqLens is a general tool for detecting long-term trends in gridded Earth-system data. Users load a variable, click any point on the map, and MarqLens answers the challenge's four questions for that point:

  • What is changing: the chosen variable.
  • Where: a map by grid cell.
  • How much: Sen's slope per year, and % change compared with a baseline.
  • Is the change significant: a Mann-Kendall test with Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation, plus Benjamini-Yekutieli control because thousands of cells are tested at once.

Each click also shows a yearly chart, the seasonal cycle, anomalies and a year-by-month heatmap.

To demonstrate it, we used one example: annual rainfall in the Amazon River basin, 2001–2024.

Benefits and intended impact
Most people only see short-term forecasts, not how their environment has shifted over decades. MarqLens shows that in one click, with no data downloading or statistics needed. It also shows how reliable each result is, in three plain-language tiers, with grey areas where the evidence is too weak.

In the Amazon example, the south-central basin and the Andean strip show signs of drying. However, 24 years cannot yet separate the extreme dry years of 2022–2024 from a lasting shift, and MarqLens states this openly.

Because the core is domain-neutral, the same tool can be pointed at temperature, vegetation, soil moisture or any region.

Tools and technologies

  • Data (example): NASA GPM IMERG Final V07 (monthly, 0.1°) and MERRA-2 skin temperature, both via NASA Giovanni. HydroBASINS for the basin boundary.
  • Code: Python with xarray, plus our own open package trendlab, which has 61 automated tests and no variable- or region-specific code.
  • App: Streamlit.
  • Development: Google Colab and GitHub.
  • AI: Claude helped with coding and method review. This is disclosed in AI_USAGE.md.

Creativity
Most trend maps colour every pixel as if every result were certain. MarqLens makes uncertainty part of the design. It also includes a Discovery mode with four guided experiences: Climate Detective, Grey Zone Mystery, Time Machine and Evidence Challenge. Other features are rainfall stripes and a year-by-year map with a play slider. An exploratory tab shows associations with ocean indices such as El Niño, worded as associations, not causes.

Factors we considered

  • Earth-observation records are often short, so we kept methods simple and tested our choices with simulations. Pre-whitening (TFPW) increased false positives, so we dropped it and documented this as a negative result.
  • In the example, satellite data has not yet been checked against ground stations.
  • Monthly data does not allow extreme-event analysis.
  • We separated the general engine (trendlab) from the example data so the pipeline is reusable.
